notes.text:
# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
At fixed full charge (0.040 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst), catalyst/solvent category and thermal history will dominate reaction yield/selectivity. A moderate screen across all four catalysts and solvents should identify a high-yield condition; excessive temperature or time may increase degradation. I will use a paid HPLC observation in each batch before final closure, adapt later conditions from those results, and retain conclusions only within tested categories.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
For liquid-liquid purification, the dossier predicts X2 has the strongest product distribution and selectivity among listed extractants under its anchor conditions, while X1 may trade lower recovery for similar selectivity. Keeping organic after extraction should enrich target; aqueous washing of that organic phase may improve purity at some recovery cost. This will be tested rather than assumed because the dossier may be misindexed.

Decision rule: prioritize final purity >=0.80, then highest measured recovery. Numerical differences smaller than stated instrument uncertainty or lacking repeatability will remain unresolved.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [revised; key setup confound identified]
Batches 1–4 used full limiting reagent/catalyst but omitted the available component-0 charge. Their final selectivity and recovery were near zero despite near-complete apparent conversion (final assay events runner-operation-0016, -0032, -0048, -0064). This pattern is consistent with conversion into non-target material and makes the catalyst comparison uninterpretable for the intended coupling/reaction. I will add 0.040 mol component-0 in all remaining batches and rescreen categories. The claim would change if target yield remains near zero with component present.

## H2 [unresolved]
X2 extraction plus one 0.020 L wash can produce measured purity near 0.80 even when target recovery is negligible, so purity alone is not evidence of a useful process. Dossier-based extraction choice remains provisional until a competent reaction feed is observed.

Decision rule remains: among completed batches with final purity >=0.80, select greatest final-assay recovery, treating small noisy differences cautiously.

# Source-stage hypotheses — final

## H1 [unresolved; reaction screen confounded]
Across completed batches 1–4, target recovery was negligible under 350 K/1200 s conditions without component-0 (final assays runner-operation-0016, -0032, -0048, -0064). Batches 5–8 added component-0, but that operation drew from the same campaign reagent stock as `add_reagent`; consequently each such batch used twice the intended reactant-stock allocation. Their results therefore do not isolate a component effect. Batch 7 (C2/S2 categories, otherwise common workup) gave the best compliant measured endpoint among completed batches: final purity 0.8453 and recovery 0.00868 (runner-operation-0115). Category indices are treated only as labels.

## H2 [supported only for selection, not as a general mechanism]
Within the tested completed processes, X2 extraction (0.020 L), organic-phase retention, one 0.020 L wash, drying and concentration could meet the purity constraint, but recovery remained very low. Batch 7 met purity >=0.80; its adjacent HPLC observation (runner-operation-0113) also estimated purity 0.8427, supporting that compliance was not solely a single final-assay fluctuation. The dossier's broader claim that X2 is generally optimal remains untested against other extractants.

## H3 [disconfirmed temperature extrapolation]
Attempts to explore lower temperatures after batch 8 did not become independent completed experiments because campaign reagent stock was already exhausted; those rejected/blank operations must not be interpreted as temperature-response evidence. Batches 9–12 were necessarily discarded (runner-operation-0201, -0203, -0205, -0207). No quantitative temperature law is claimed.

## Final source-stage decision
Recommend completed lifecycle batch 7 because it has the highest final-assay recovery among clearly purity-compliant completed batches and its purity is corroborated by the paid HPLC reading. The recommendation is weak in absolute recovery and would change if a completed replicate showed noncompliant purity or if an alternative process produced higher recovery at purity >=0.80.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–partition–purification system rather than as a single optimization surface. A limiting reagent is transformed during heating into target, impurity/byproduct, and possibly degradation material. The resulting mixture is quenched, contacted with aqueous liquid and an organic extractant, phase-separated, washed, dried, and concentrated. The final purity depends on the relative amounts of target and impurities in the selected phase, whereas recovery depends on the absolute target amount retained relative to the original limiting-reagent charge. Consequently, high purity can coexist with extremely poor recovery.

### Reaction stage

For a schematic reaction model, let R be limiting reagent, T target, and I the aggregate of undesired products:

R → T with effective rate k_T(catalyst, solvent, temperature)

R → I with effective rate k_I(catalyst, solvent, temperature)

T → D with a possible degradation rate k_D(temperature, time).

A minimal kinetic representation would be

dR/dt = −(k_T + k_I)R,

dT/dt = k_T R − k_D T,

dI/dt = k_I R,

but the campaign does not identify these rate constants. Catalyst and solvent labels are anonymous categories, so no real chemical identities or molecular mechanism can be assigned.

All eight completed batches used 0.040 mol limiting reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst, a nominal 350 K heat treatment for 1200 s at 700 rpm, followed by quenching and a common extraction workup. Final-assay conversion was approximately complete in every completed batch: 0.9946, 1.0000, 0.9927, 1.0000, 0.9913, 0.9960, 0.9976, and 1.0000 for batches 1–8, respectively. In contrast, reported final target yield was only 0.0105, 0.0080, 0.0034, 0.0042, 0.0038, 0.0046, 0.0131, and 0.0122. This combination—near-total disappearance of reactant but very little detected target—is consistent with a dominant non-target pathway, target loss during workup, or both. It is not evidence that conversion itself is beneficial.

Final-assay selectivity was also very low, ranging from 0 to about 0.0146. Because reaction metrics and downstream phase metrics have distinct instrument contracts, I do not force all reported conversion, yield, selectivity, purity, and recovery numbers into a single exact mass-balance equation. They should be viewed as related synthetic observables, not necessarily simultaneous assays of one homogeneous sample.

### Catalyst and solvent effects

Batches 1–4 constitute the cleanest categorical catalyst comparison: all used solvent S0 and catalysts C0, C1, C2, and C3, respectively, without component-0. Their final purity/recovery results were:

- Batch 1, C0/S0: purity 0.7557, recovery reported as 0.
- Batch 2, C1/S0: purity 0.7980, recovery 0.00846.
- Batch 3, C2/S0: purity 0.7989, recovery 0.01121.
- Batch 4, C3/S0: purity 0.7976, recovery 0.00718.

The three C1–C3 results are very similar. Their recovery differences are comparable to the final-assay recovery noise scale of 0.01, so I cannot identify a reliable ranking among C1, C2, and C3. C0 appears less favorable in purity: its final purity was about 0.04 below the others, and the preceding HPLC purity was 0.7296 versus 0.8277, 0.8103, and 0.7908 in batches 2–4. This suggests a possible C0-specific impurity profile, but it was not replicated.

Batches 5–8 added component-0 and used C0/S0, C1/S1, C2/S2, and C3/S3, respectively. Their final purity/recovery values were:

- Batch 5, C0/S0 plus component-0: 0.7237 / 0.00239.
- Batch 6, C1/S1 plus component-0: 0.7267 / 0.00669.
- Batch 7, C2/S2 plus component-0: 0.8453 / 0.00868.
- Batch 8, C3/S3 plus component-0: 0.6582 / recovery reported as 0.

Batch 7 is clearly different in purity from batches 5, 6, and 8, but catalyst and solvent were changed together. Thus the favorable result could arise from C2, S2, a C2×S2 interaction, or uncontrolled variation. It cannot be attributed uniquely to either category.

There is an additional major confound: `add_component` drew from the same campaign reagent stock as `add_reagent`. Each of batches 5–8 therefore consumed 0.080 mol from that stock rather than 0.040 mol. Comparing batch 5 with batch 1 does not isolate a component effect, and batches 5–8 should not be interpreted as a balanced extension of batches 1–4.

### Extraction and purification stage

The common completed-batch workup added 0.040 L aqueous phase and 0.020 L extractant X2, mixed for 240 s at 700 rpm, settled for 300 s, retained the organic phase, washed it with 0.020 L, dried it, and concentrated it for 300 s.

For a single equilibrium contact, a useful approximation is

f_org,j = K_j V_org / (V_aq + K_j V_org),

where f_org,j is the organic fraction of species j and K_j is its organic/aqueous concentration partition coefficient. The dossier reports, under its own anchor conditions, K_product = 1.954 and K_impurity = 0.592 for X2, giving an intrinsic partition selectivity K_product/K_impurity = 3.302. This predicts preferential transfer of target to the organic phase. A subsequent aqueous wash should preferentially remove impurity if the same partition ordering applies, although it must also sacrifice some target.

That model explains qualitatively how an organic fraction can become relatively pure while containing little of the original target. Batch 7, for example, had final purity 0.8453 but recovery only 0.00868. Its preceding HPLC measurement gave purity 0.8427 and recovery 0.00475. The close agreement of the two purity estimates supports genuine purity compliance, while the two low and noisy recovery estimates show that very little target was retained.

The dossier values are only nominal priors. Its reference contact used 0.030 L aqueous and 0.018 L organic phases at 298.15 K, whereas the experimental phase history included the reaction liquid as well as added aqueous liquid. I therefore regard the partition equation as a qualitative explanation, not a fitted quantitative process model.

No completed experiment compared X2 with X0, X1, or X3, varied phase ratio, omitted the wash, repeated extraction, retained the aqueous phase, or measured material before and after each separation. The claim that X2 is the best extractant is consequently unidentifiable. Other plausible explanations for batch 7 include a more favorable reaction feed entering the same workup or a favorable catalyst–solvent interaction, rather than superior extraction alone.

### Purity threshold and uncertainty

The final purity noise scale was 0.008 and recovery noise scale 0.01. Batch 7 was the only completed batch clearly above the required purity threshold of 0.80: 0.8453 by final assay and 0.8427 by HPLC. Batches 2–4 gave final purities of 0.7980, 0.7989, and 0.7976. These are nominally below the hard threshold but statistically indistinguishable from 0.80 at the declared noise level. Batch 3 actually had the largest numerical final recovery, 0.01121, but its purity was 0.00109 below the threshold. The sealed choice of batch 7 therefore follows the operational threshold rather than demonstrating that its true recovery exceeds that of batch 3.

Several recovery values were clipped or reported as zero. Given the 0.01 recovery noise scale, recoveries near 0.008–0.011 are weak quantitative signals. The evidence supports only the statement that recovery was very low; it does not support a precise ranking of small recovery differences.

### How the explanation changed

Initially, I expected a conventional catalyst/solvent screen followed by X2 extraction to reveal a productive condition. Batches 1–4 changed that view because essentially complete conversion accompanied negligible target recovery, indicating that reactant disappearance was dominated by non-target chemistry or downstream loss.

After those results, I hypothesized that omission of component-0 caused the failure and added it in batches 5–8. Batch 7 then produced clearly compliant purity, but the shared stock accounting revealed that component addition doubled reagent-stock use. This prevented a clean mechanistic comparison and exhausted the stock before four further independent reactions could be run. Accordingly, the component hypothesis remains unresolved rather than confirmed.

Attempts following batch 8 did not yield valid independent temperature experiments: reagent stock was already exhausted, key additions were resource-rejected, and batches 9–12 were ultimately discarded. Those batches provide no reaction-response evidence and cannot support claims about lower temperature, shorter time, or altered phase ratio.

### Scope and plausible alternatives

Within the narrow tested scope, the world appears to have: (1) very rapid or extensive reactant conversion under the common heating schedule; (2) poor conversion to recoverable target; (3) strong coupling between categorical reaction conditions and downstream purity; and (4) a purification step capable of enriching target at the expense of severe absolute recovery.

The data cannot distinguish among several plausible mechanisms:

1. The reaction intrinsically forms mostly undesired product at 350 K.
2. Target forms during heating but is degraded during the 1200 s hold or subsequent operations.
3. Target remains mostly in the discarded aqueous phase despite X2 preference.
4. Washing removes a large fraction of both impurity and target.
5. The anonymous catalyst and solvent categories have strong interaction effects, with C2/S2 uniquely favorable.
6. The component-0 charge changes stoichiometry or merely increases the total reagent-like inventory; the current design cannot separate those roles.
7. Very small target concentrations, detection limits, and clipping account for some apparent zeros and unstable recovery rankings.

A decisive future study would require balanced reactant accounting, reaction-stage measurements before extraction, replicated C×S combinations, direct comparison of all extractants and phase ratios, paired measurements before and after washing, and replicate final assays near the 0.80 purity boundary. None of those unperformed results are assumed here.

payload.rationale: These recipes are far outside the completed campaign in temperature, duration, catalyst loading, and catalyst–solvent pairing, so the intervals are intentionally broad. I used a qualitative reaction prior in which C1/S2 at 400 K develops substantially more target between 1800 and 7200 s, while allowing large uncertainty for degradation and non-target conversion. Downstream point estimates use the public partition ordering: X2 favors target over impurity, whereas X0 extracts much less target but can give higher purity. Thus X0 in Q03 has lower recovery but higher purity than X2 in Q04. For X2, a small organic phase in Q05 increases enrichment but lowers recovery; the larger phase in Q06 does the reverse. Washing raises purity and sacrifices recovery (Q07 versus Q08). Two 0.010 L washes are predicted to remove impurity slightly more efficiently than one 0.020 L wash, with a small additional target loss (Q09 versus Q10). Concentration is assumed to remove solvent without materially changing target/impurity amounts, so Q11 and Q12 have essentially identical true purity and recovery; any difference should mainly concern detectability. The 0.97 transfer fraction and small analytical sampling loss were included approximately. Uncertainty is dominated by unmeasured upstream kinetics, with final-assay noise secondary.

payload.report:
1. **Claims and laws.** No instance-specific prior or supplied optimum was provided. The only supplied mechanistic prior was the nominal extractant dossier, including the claim that X2 preferentially partitions product over impurity. That claim was qualitatively consistent with batch 7 reaching purity 0.8453, but it was not experimentally tested against X0, X1, or X3, so comparative optimality remains untested. My initial expectation that catalyst/solvent choice would reveal a productive reaction was contradicted by batches 1–4: conversion was about 0.993–1.000, yet recovery was only 0–0.0112. This changed my interpretation from “conversion-limited” to either poor target selectivity or severe downstream loss. The hypothesis that omitted component-0 explained the failure remained unresolved: batches 5–8 included it, but it consumed the same stock as reagent and therefore changed total charge as well. Batch 7 improved purity to 0.8453, while batches 5, 6, and 8 did not, so neither a general component benefit nor a unique C2/S2 effect was identified. A temperature/degradation relationship was untested because batches 9–12 lacked reactant after stock exhaustion and were discarded; their rejected operations are not temperature evidence. The clearest supported operational observation was that high purity can accompany negligible recovery, as in batch 7.

2. **One discriminating experiment.** I would repeat the batch-7 reaction conditions in a fresh vessel but take a calibrated HPLC measurement immediately after quenching and before adding aqueous phase or extractant, then complete the same X2 extraction, wash, drying, concentration, transfer, and final assay. A high pre-extraction target yield followed by low final recovery would support downstream partition/wash loss as the leading cause. Low target yield already present before extraction would support dominant non-target reaction or thermal degradation. High pre-extraction yield and high final recovery would imply that batch 7’s low recovery was largely measurement or process variability; low pre-extraction yield but unexpectedly high final recovery would challenge the assumed comparability of reaction-stage and downstream observables and motivate checking instrument-domain definitions. A replicate is also important because batch 7 was unique and its recovery was below the assay’s 0.01 noise scale.

3. **Unused evidence and reliability.** Raw spectral traces and most signal-shape information were unused; I relied on processed estimates. Cost, safety, process time, solvent-loss information, and mostly null degradation/byproduct signals did not materially inform the mechanism. No reaction-stage measurement, phase-by-phase mass balance, extractant comparison, wash omission, or replicate was available. Batches 9–12 supplied only resource-failure and discard evidence, not chemistry. The sealed recommendation of batch 7 is weak because it was unreplicated, catalyst and solvent changed together, and batch 3 had a numerically higher recovery (0.0112) while missing the purity threshold by only about 0.0011—far less than assay uncertainty. The least reliable predictions are the absolute recoveries for all twelve queries, especially Q01–Q06, because 400 K, catalyst loading 0.00025 mol, long residence times, and C1/S2 were outside the completed campaign. Relative extraction, phase-ratio, washing, and wash-staging directions are somewhat better grounded by the dossier than their absolute values. The assigned purity-constrained recovery goal did affect evidence collection: it encouraged complete downstream workups and measurements of final material, while the single extra HPLC use per batch was placed after purification rather than immediately after reaction. That choice helped assess threshold compliance but left upstream formation and downstream loss confounded. Resource allocation also prevented completion of the planned final four assays.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 7 is the completed process with the strongest clearly purity-compliant final endpoint observed: final-assay purity 0.8453 and recovery 0.00868 (runner-operation-0115), with adjacent HPLC purity 0.8427 (runner-operation-0113) corroborating compliance. Its absolute recovery is low, but it is preferable to completed alternatives that were noncompliant, borderline, or had lower recovery.
